# *bmassa* <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="bmassa logo" />

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/STABLE-uv/bmassa/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/STABLE-uv/bmassa/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

*bmassa* estimates the mean individual mass and the biomass of aquatic
taxa (phytoplankton, zooplankton, macroinvertebrates, fish and amphibians)
from abundance data, with prediction intervals. Hierarchical models fitted
to published compilations and data sets predict each taxon from its own
reference data or, when it has none, from its closest relatives, and the
interval widens with the substitution. All the estimates are in one
currency: wet mass (mg) by default, or dry mass, ash-free dry mass, carbon or
energy, converted from the currency of each model with the uncertainty of the
conversion factors.

## Installation

From GitHub, with its dependencies:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("STABLE-uv/bmassa", dependencies = TRUE)
```

*bmassa* needs R (>= 3.6.0) and the R packages *stats* (R Core Team 2024)
and *withr* (Hester et al. 2022). *curl* (Ooms 2023) and *jsonlite* (Ooms
2014) are needed only by `standardize_taxa()`, which queries the Catalogue of
Life through the GBIF API.

## Example

Two tables: the taxon units (a taxon, or a taxon in one life stage and
sex, with its classification and its counting unit) and their abundances by
site (and date, if any). A third, optional table holds the lengths: usually
the mean length of a unit, and the lengths of individuals where they were
measured (one row per individual or per length class, with the number of
individuals `n`). A length without `site` applies to all the samples of the
unit, one with `site` to that site (and one with `date`, to that sample), and
each sample takes the most specific. Constructed example data shipped with
the package:

```{r data}
library(bmassa)
tx <- example_survey$taxa
ab <- example_survey$abundance
ln <- example_survey$lengths
tx[c(1, 8, 13, 19, 20), c("taxon_id", "broad_group", "genus", "species", "life_stage",
                          "count_unit")]
head(ab, 3)
ln
```

Here the chub (`t17`) has a mean length in each site, and the *Gammarus*
(`t13`) of site L1 were measured by length class.

For your own list of names, `standardize_taxa()` returns this
classification and the identifier of each taxon (`col_id`) from the
Catalogue of Life (COL XR); it needs internet.

Before estimating, the taxonomic level from which each taxon will come, and
the factor by which the median is divided and multiplied to get its 95 %
interval:

```{r coverage}
check_coverage(tx, ln)
```

The mean individual mass of a population of each taxon and the biomass of
each row, in wet mass (mg) by default. With lengths, the back-transformation
of the length-mass relations has to be chosen: `"lognormal"` gives the mean
mass of the individuals of each length, which biomass needs:

```{r estimate}
est <- estimate_biomass(ab, tx, ln, bias_correction = "lognormal")
est
e <- as.data.frame(est)
print(e[e$site == "L1", c("taxon_id", "method", "match_level", "length_mm", "ind_median",
                          "ind_lower", "ind_upper", "unit")], digits = 3)
```

In another currency, here carbon in µg, with the uncertainty of the
conversion factors (amphibians have too few factors in the reference data:
they go to dry mass and energy with the values of frogs and toads of US EPA
1993, but not to carbon). `estimate_biomass(ab, tx, ln, bias_correction =
"lognormal", currency = "carbon", unit = "ug")` gives the same:

```{r carbon}
est_c <- convert_currency(est, to = "carbon", unit = "ug")
ec <- as.data.frame(est_c)
print(ec[ec$site == "L1", c("taxon_id", "converted_from", "ind_median", "ind_lower",
                            "ind_upper", "unit")], digits = 3)
```

Totals by site and group, by simulation with shared draws: two taxa
estimated from the same family, or the same taxon in two sites, have
correlated errors:

```{r totals}
tot <- summarize_biomass(est_c, by = c("site", "broad_group"), na_rm = TRUE, seed = 1)
print(tot[, c("site", "broad_group", "biomass_unit", "biomass_mean", "biomass_lower",
              "biomass_upper", "n_missing")], digits = 3)
```

The size structure of each sample: the mean and median mass of the
individuals, weighted by their abundances, and the shares of the individuals
and of the biomass in size classes, with the share of individuals without a
size; taxa known only by their mean size make the median and the classes
approximations (`approximation`):

```{r size}
sz <- summarize_size(est, by = c("site", "broad_group"), seed = 1)
print(as.data.frame(sz)[, c("site", "broad_group", "mean_size", "median_size",
                            "share_excluded", "approximation")], digits = 3)
```

The draws themselves, for models that use the biomass of every taxon (such
as the energy fluxes of a food web): the mean individual mass and the
biomass of every row in every draw, with the same shared errors as the
totals. Here all the groups per square metre of each site
(`convert_abundance()`, from the depth of each site), so that they can be
added up, with the populations of each habitat apart (`population_by`):

```{r simulate, warning = FALSE}
sites <- data.frame(site = c("L1", "L2"), depth = c(1.5, 0.8), depth_unit = "m")
ab_m2 <- convert_abundance(ab, to = "m2", sites = sites)
ab_m2$habitat <- ifelse(ab_m2$site == "L1", "lake", "spring")
est_w <- estimate_biomass(ab_m2, tx, ln, bias_correction = "lognormal")
sim <- simulate(est_w, nsim = 1000, seed = 1, population_by = "habitat")
d <- as.data.frame(sim, draws = 1:2)
print(head(d[, c("draw", "site", "taxon_id", "habitat", "ind_mass", "biomass",
                 "biomass_unit")]), digits = 3)
```

## Methods and decisions

- The models were fitted with the R package *lme4* (Bates et al. 2015) to the
  reference data (one per domain and kind of data): masses without lengths
  with nested random effects by taxonomic level, length-mass relations with
  random intercepts and slopes by level and length type, and conversion
  factors between currencies with nested random effects. The package predicts
  from their tables with base R; `get_reference()` returns them.
- A taxon is matched by its `col_id`, if given, and otherwise by name and
  rank, from its lowest rank upwards, to the taxonomy of the Catalogue of
  Life (COL XR) used for the reference.
- The interval is for the mean individual mass of a population of the taxon:
  it includes the uncertainty of the model, of the taxonomic substitution and
  the variation between populations and between sources, but not the error
  of the abundances.
- The totals and `simulate()` share the errors of rows estimated from the
  same node of the reference, of the same population and of the same
  conversion factors; `simulate()` returns the draws of the totals, row by
  row.
- Insects without lengths and without a stage are taken as larvae, and
  copepods as adults (their copepodites and nauplii are fixed contrasts);
  fish without lengths are estimated as whole populations (all sizes), with
  wide intervals; amphibians only after metamorphosis (larvae are not
  estimated), and without lengths only when declared adults.
- Phytoplankton counted in natural units takes the natural units of the
  reference, often single cells or small groups in colonial genera; give
  `cells_per_unit` for colonies counted whole.
- Lengths outside those of the reference relations of a taxon use its
  closest relative that covers them, and are not extrapolated unless
  `extrapolate = TRUE`.
- With the lengths of individuals, the mean mass is the mean of their
  masses, without assuming a distribution of lengths; with a mean length,
  its spread (`length_sd` or `length_cv`) corrects the mass of the mean
  length, smaller than the mean mass.
- The models predict phytoplankton biovolume, the dry mass of invertebrates
  and the wet mass of fish and amphibians; every row is then converted to the
  currency asked for, with the conversion models (a row that cannot reach it
  is not estimated, with the reason).
- The vignettes: `vignette("bmassa")` goes through the workflow and the
  decisions, `vignette("tuesday-lake")` compares the predictions with the
  masses and biomasses measured in Tuesday Lake, and
  `vignette("azoxystrobin")` goes from the raw counts of a mesocosm
  experiment (Amador et al. 2024) to the effect of a fungicide on biomass,
  with a generalized linear mixed model. The cross-validation of the
  intervals is in the source repository
  (`dev/validation/cross_validation.md`).

## Data sources

```{r sources}
s <- cite_sources()
knitr::kable(s[, c("source_id", "citation", "licence")])
```

The fish data of NEON are used as its data policy asks: this material is
based in part upon work supported by the National Ecological Observatory
Network (NEON), a program sponsored by the U.S. National Science Foundation
(NSF) and operated under cooperative agreement by Battelle.

## Status

Version 0.5.0, not on CRAN. In cross-validation, the 95 %
intervals cover 92-97 % of new populations of species in the reference and
94-97 % of species left out. Masses without lengths are much more uncertain
(the median is divided and multiplied by a factor of about 7 to 40 for the
95 % interval of a new population) than masses from lengths (a factor of 1.2
to 3.3): measure lengths where possible.

## Known limitations

- Benthic invertebrates without lengths are predicted as population means:
  the masses of individual prey of Moreau et al. (2021) are corrected by a
  factor of about 6 estimated from the few families they share with the
  population means of Hrycik et al. (2024), so the estimates of benthic taxa
  measured only by Moreau depend on that correction (95 % interval 3.6 to
  11).
- Copepods without a stage are taken as adults: a count of a species that
  includes its copepodites is overestimated (1.4 to 3.6 times in the test
  with Tuesday Lake); give the copepodites as rows of their own.
- Phytoplankton counted in natural units goes to carbon and energy only
  with `cells_per_unit`; without it, only to wet mass.
- The conversion factors have two to four sources per model, too few to
  estimate the variation between sources: with each source left out in
  turn, 61-66 % of the wet to dry mass and dry mass to carbon factors of
  invertebrates fall inside their 95 % intervals.
- Amphibian larvae are not estimated, with or without lengths.
- Fish without lengths: the mean masses of populations come from Iberian
  streams (Arranz et al. 2022), the Mekong (Koning et al. 2024) and streams
  and lakes of the United States (NEON, 2016-2024), mostly small fish caught
  by electrofishing: populations of large adults (stocked fish, catches of
  fisheries) are underestimated, and orders absent from them take the mean
  of their class.
- There is no dry mass or AFDM of phytoplankton, no AFDM or carbon of
  amphibians, and no energy of masses with shell: in those currencies, those
  rows are not estimated.
- Detritus, periphyton and macrophytes are outside the scope of the
  package.
